transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, honestly, it’s a whole mess of things, but what finally got me here—what really pushed me to make this appointment, which, by the way, I almost missed because I was halfway through reorganizing my entire toolbox by wrench size and metal finish—is that I just can’t keep my focus on anything for more than a few seconds. I’m an electrician, right? I do a lot of residential and some light commercial work, and I have to write up these estimates and fill out code forms. It’s important stuff, you know? You mess up a code form, and the inspector is breathing down your neck, the client is mad, the whole schedule gets pushed back. 

But lately, I’ll sit down to do an estimate, and... bam. Someone drops a tool across the room, or I hear a drill, and I’m suddenly thinking about how I could design a better, quieter drill motor. Or my phone buzzes with a text, not even an important one, just like, a buddy talking about the game, and suddenly I’m off on this massive tangent about how we need to rewire the whole workshop to put in a better sound system and a new flat screen. And then I’m sketching out the schematics for *that* instead of finishing the estimate. I’ve got all these brilliant ideas for the shop, really top-tier stuff, but because every little noise or thought pulls me completely off track, the actual paying jobs are starting to get all mixed up. I’m sending the wrong quotes to the wrong people, or forgetting to finish them entirely. It’s just... everything catches my attention all at once, you know? It's like my brain is a radio scanning every station at maximum volume.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Fidgeting? Doc, I don't even get to the point of sitting still long enough to actually fidget. If my butt hits a chair, my skin practically starts crawling. I’ve just been going absolutely nonstop lately. Like, I’ll be out at a job site in the morning—maybe doing a rough-in for a new residential build, pulling wire, bending conduit, all the heavy physical stuff—and then instead of taking a breather or grabbing lunch like a normal person, I'm speeding across town to knock out two or three bids. 

And then when I finally get back to the workshop, I can't just sit at the desk to do the paperwork. I've got these test panels set up in the back, and I just started completely rewiring them because I had this brilliant thought about optimizing the breaker layout for faster troubleshooting. But the thing is, before I even finish stripping the wires for the test panel, I'm already pulling out components for this new home-automation idea I had. It's this whole smart relay system I'm designing, really cutting-edge stuff that integrates everything, but I’ve got like four different prototypes started on the workbench and none of them finished. 

I just keep jumping from one project to the next because... well, sitting still just feels like a massive waste of time. It really does. There’s so much to do, so many ideas constantly flowing, so if I try to just sit there and relax or look at a screen, I feel this crazy electric buzz in my legs and I just have to get back up and keep moving. It's like my motor is idling too high to ever actually put it in park.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?

Impulse? I mean, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive, not like, doing crazy stuff for no reason. It's more like... when I get an idea, I just know it's a good one, so why wait, right? Like, I don't see the point in sitting around debating it when the answer is right there in front of me. 

Take last Thursday, for example. I was at the hardware supply house, just picking up some Romex and a few junction boxes for a kitchen remodel I'm supposed to be doing. Standard stuff, right? But then I saw they had this massive sale on commercial-grade LED troffers. I'm talking like, top-of-the-line, dimmable, color-tunable panels. And immediately, my brain just clicks, and I'm like, "The workshop needs these." Because the lighting in there is terrible, honestly, it's just these old fluorescent tubes that hum and give me a headache, and if I'm going to be doing all this high-level design work and building these prototypes, I need optimal lighting. 

So, I didn't even really think about the budget for the kitchen job or the fact that my truck was already pretty full. I just bought twelve of them. Twelve commercial fixtures. I maxed out the company card right there at the counter. The guy at the register, Dave—I've known Dave for years—he even asked me, "Hey man, you doing a warehouse job?" And I just laughed and said, "Nope, just upgrading the command center!" 

And then, of course, I had to figure out how to strap them to the roof rack of my van because they wouldn't fit inside with all my other gear, and I spent the whole drive back thinking about the wiring schematic to put them all on a three-way switch system with smart relays. I mean, my business partner was pretty ticked off when he saw the credit card alert, and yeah, maybe I should have run it by him first since we technically needed that credit line for the kitchen materials, but... I don't know if that's acting without thinking about consequences. To me, the consequence is just having an awesome, perfectly lit workshop, you know? It just made sense in the moment. I just move fast when I see an opportunity. I don't know if I'd call it an impulse problem.
Do you often find yourself talking more than others in social situations?

Talk more than others? I mean, I guess I do talk a lot, but it’s just because I have so much to say, you know? Like, my brain is just moving so fast, making all these connections that other people just aren’t seeing. 

Take last weekend, for example. I went to this barbecue at my buddy Mike’s house—Mike’s a plumber, good guy, but a little slow on the uptake sometimes. Anyway, he’s got this group of guys over, mostly guys in the trades, and they’re all just standing around drinking beers and talking about, I don't know, sports or whatever. And I get there, and I’m just fired up. I had just come from the shop, where I was working on that smart relay system I told you about, and I was just buzzing with all these ideas about how we could integrate it into residential builds to completely revolutionize home energy efficiency. 

So I start explaining it to them, right? I’m breaking down the schematics, the load balancing, the whole nine yards. And I’m talking, and I’m talking, and I’m just so passionate about it because it’s honestly a game-changer. And I notice that they’re all just kind of staring at me. Like, nobody else is saying a word. Mike’s just holding his spatula, looking at me like I grew a second head. And I’m thinking, "Come on guys, keep up!" But they just couldn’t. They were just totally lost in the sauce. 

And it’s not just that one time, either. It’s like, whenever I’m in a group, I just feel this... this pressure to get all my thoughts out before I forget them or before someone else changes the subject to something boring. I’ll be talking to my business partner, Greg, about a job, and I’ll just go off on this massive tangent about a new way to route the conduit that would save us like, 15% on materials, but it requires this whole new bending technique that I invented, and before I know it, I’ve been talking for twenty minutes straight and Greg hasn’t even gotten a word in edgewise. He actually told me the other day to "take a breath," which honestly kind of ticked me off because I don't need to take a breath, I need him to listen to what I’m saying because it’s important!

So yeah, I guess I do talk more than other people. But I don't think it's a bad thing. I just have a lot of really good ideas, and I need to share them, you know? It's just that most people can't process information as fast as I can dish it out right now. They're all just operating on dial-up, and I'm on gigabit fiber.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or having trouble waiting for your turn in conversations?

Interrupting? No, I wouldn't say I do that. I mean, I definitely let people finish their thoughts, even if I already know exactly where they're going with it. I don't cut people off. 

Like, just yesterday, I was on site with this new apprentice we brought on, Josh. Good kid, hard worker, but he was trying to explain to me why he decided to run the half-inch EMT conduit this completely bizarre way around the HVAC return in a basement remodel we're doing. And I just stood there, and I listened to his whole entire explanation. I didn't interrupt him once. I let him talk about the floor joists, and the duct clearance, and how he thought he was avoiding a plumbing stack. 

But the thing is, while he's talking, my brain is already ten steps ahead, right? Like, within two seconds of him pointing at the ceiling, I've already mapped out the entire circuit in my head, calculated the voltage drop, realized he's going to completely exceed the 360-degree bend rule if he keeps going that route, and I’ve already designed a completely different path that saves us at least ten feet of pipe and a handful of fittings. 

But I didn't cut him off! I let him get it all out. It's just that the absolute second he stops talking, I'm immediately coming in with the actual solution. Boom, right away. So maybe to some people it *feels* like I'm not waiting my turn, just because I respond so fast? Like, I don't need to sit there and stroke my chin and ponder what they said for five minutes like Greg does. I already processed the whole thing while they were still getting the words out of their mouth. 

So no, I really don't think I interrupt. I just have a really fast response time, you know? Once they're done talking, the floor is open, and I'm just ready to go.
Do you often have trouble completing tasks once you've started them?

Trouble completing tasks? Well, I wouldn't say I have *trouble* completing them, it's more like... there's just so much to do, and I'm doing all of it at once. I mean, I've been going absolutely nonstop lately. It's like I'm running on a completely different frequency than everyone else. 

Just to give you a picture of what my week has looked like—I'm bouncing from job site to job site, right? I've got the kitchen remodel in the heights, a service upgrade across town, and I'm squeezing in bids for three other commercial jobs in between. But that's not even the half of it. Because the second I get back to the shop, I'm not winding down. I'm right back into it, rewiring these test panels we have set up. 

And, okay, yeah, maybe I do start a new home-automation idea before the last one is totally buttoned up, but that's just because the ideas keep coming, and they're all so good. Like, I'll be halfway through wiring a smart relay for a lighting sequence, and suddenly I realize, "Wait, I can integrate this with the HVAC zone dampers using a low-voltage trigger," and boom, I'm pulling new wire for that. Sitting still just feels like a massive waste of time right now. Why would I stop and just... be done, when I could be making the whole system ten times better? 

My business partner, Greg, he gets so hung up on checking off one box before moving to the next. He's like, "Did you finish the rough-in on the Smith job?" And I'm like, "Greg, I did most of it, but I also drafted a completely new schematic for a whole-house audio integration that we can upsell them on, and I started building the prototype on the workbench." He doesn't get it. He thinks I'm scattered, but I'm just operating at maximum capacity. I'm getting more done in a day than he does in a week, even if every single little wire nut isn't tightened down on the first project before I start the second one. It's just... activity, you know? Constant, productive activity. I can't just stop.
Do you often have trouble keeping your workspace or living space organized?

Organized? No, no, definitely not. If anything, I’m hyper-organized right now. Like, my system is absolutely flawless. Greg—my partner, I mentioned him—he walked past my workbench yesterday and made some smart comment about it looking like a bomb went off in a copper mine, but he just doesn’t possess the visual-spatial processing to understand how I’ve laid it out. It’s not a mess, it’s a highly efficient radial workflow! 

I mean, think about it. Why would I put the wire strippers and the linesman pliers back in the main toolbox across the room every single time I use them? That’s just wasted motion. So I have them exactly fourteen inches from my dominant hand, right next to the multimeter, which is calibrated and ready to go. And the components! I spent, I don't know, maybe five hours the other night—I was just completely in the zone, couldn't stop—just totally reorganizing all my fasteners and connectors. I dumped out all the old plastic coffee cans Greg uses, which is just a prehistoric way to store things, by the way. I sorted every single Wago lever nut, every standard wire nut, every insulated crimp terminal... I even separated the half-inch EMT set-screw couplings from the compression couplings, which Greg always mixes together and it drives me absolutely insane when I'm up on an A-frame ladder and I blindly grab the wrong one out of my pouch.

And my work van? Oh man, my van is a masterpiece right now. I actually ripped out the factory shelving this past weekend. Completely gutted the whole back end. I realized the weight distribution was totally off, which was affecting the suspension and the gas mileage, plus the spool racks were in the worst possible spot for pulling anything heavier than 12-gauge wire. So I custom-fabricated this whole new modular rack out of scrap unistrut and spring nuts. It holds the 10-gauge, the 12-gauge, the thermostat wire, all on these frictionless axles I rigged up. I can pull three different colors of THHN simultaneously without even climbing into the back of the truck! It’s beautiful. 

So, no, I don't have trouble keeping things organized at all. I’m actually revolutionizing how we store our gear. If Greg would just let me do his van, we’d probably cut our daily load-in time by twenty percent, easy. I've tried explaining the math to him, but he’s just too stubborn to see the vision. But yeah, my spaces are perfectly sorted. Exactly how I need them.
Do you ever feel bad or guilty about how you're acting or the decisions you're making?

Guilty? No. No, why would I feel guilty? I mean, you only feel guilty if you're doing something wrong, right? Or if you're making bad decisions. And right now, I am making the best decisions I have ever made in my entire life. I am literally carrying this business on my back, optimizing everything we do, so there is absolutely nothing to feel bad about. 

I mean, I guess... I don't know, maybe Greg gets a little annoyed sometimes because I'm moving so fast and he just cannot keep up with my pace. Like with the van, when I gutted the back of it this weekend to build that custom unistrut rack I was telling you about. He was actually kind of ticked off on Monday morning because he couldn't find his old rusted hole-saw kit that I threw out, and he said I should have asked him before I completely re-engineered the company vehicle. But I didn't feel bad about it. Not even for a single second. Because once I actually sit him down and show him the math, the actual time studies I've been doing on our material loading and unloading, he is going to realize I just saved us thousands of dollars a year in wasted labor. 

So, no, I don't feel bad. If anything, it's the exact opposite. I feel completely justified in everything I'm doing right now because I can see the big picture and nobody else can. I'm operating at absolute peak performance, seeing all the angles, fixing problems before anyone else even realizes they are problems. Why would anyone feel guilty about being the only one who actually knows how to get things done right? It just wouldn't make any sense to feel bad about that.
Do you often have trouble controlling your emotions in social situations?

Emotions? I mean, look, I wouldn't call it having trouble controlling them, it's more just that my energy is so incredible right now, and people just aren't on my wavelength. Like, I’ll be in this big, pumped-up mood, right? Just firing on all cylinders, feeling fantastic. We had a little get-together this past weekend—just some of the guys from the shop, a couple of the new apprentices, my wife—and I was laying out this massive vision I have for the business. Because I realized, if we just restructure our licensing and jump on the new tax incentives, I was talking like our little shop is about to become the main solar outfit in town. I mean, the math is undeniable. I had it all mapped out, showing them how we could completely corner the residential solar-plus-storage market within six months. I was so excited, just buzzing with how huge this is going to be for us. 

But then, you know, someone will interrupt. If my wife or one of the apprentices questions the plan—like, "Oh, do we have the capital for that?" or "What about our current service contracts?"—just these tiny, small-minded, insignificant details when I am literally handing them a goldmine... yeah, I can flip. I mean, I just snap and get sharp with them over nothing. Well, it's nothing in the grand scheme of things, but in the moment, it's like they're throwing sand in the gears of a Ferrari! 

I actually told one of the apprentices to stick to fetching conduit and let the adults handle the million-dollar business strategies. Which, okay, maybe that was a little intense for a casual Saturday cookout. My wife got pretty upset with me about how I talked to him, and she pulled me aside, but I just... I get so elevated and so locked into the big picture that if anyone puts up a roadblock, I just blast right through it. I don't have the patience for the negativity or the hesitation, you know? It's like, either get on the rocket ship or get out of the way! So, yeah, I guess in social situations, if someone kills the momentum when I'm feeling that good, I definitely have a very short fuse.
Do you feel like your current way of thinking and behaving is causing problems in your personal or work life?

I mean, I wouldn't call them problems, but if you ask anyone else around me right now, they are acting like the sky is falling. It is incredibly frustrating because I am trying to elevate us and everyone else is just dragging their feet. 

Take work, for instance. I have been taking on way more jobs because, like I said, my capacity is just massive right now. I can visualize the entire wiring schematic for a commercial build before I even step on site. But because I am moving so fast and trying to juggle all these massive contracts, clients have started complaining. They are calling the shop and whining about missed details and mixed-up scheduling. Like last week on the Henderson job, they got all bent out of shape because I had us doing the rough-in on a Tuesday but I also told the drywall guys to come in, and it was a whole overlapping mess. Just a minor scheduling thing because I was trying to compress a three-week job into four days to maximize our profit margins. But now they are leaving these long voicemails about missed details, which is ridiculous because I am just prioritizing the macro over the micro. 

And the apprentices? The guys I practically trained from day one? They do not even trust my direction the way they used to. I will tell them to run a dedicated circuit a certain way to save time, a totally innovative way to route the wire that I figured out late one night, and they just look at me like I am speaking a foreign language. They hesitate. They are second-guessing me, asking if it is up to code, whispering behind my back when we are at the supply house. I am literally handing them the future of electrical contracting and they are acting like I have lost my mind. 

But the absolute worst part is at home. My wife and I cannot even be in the same room right now without it turning into a fight. It is just constant arguments about the mortgage and the business. She is looking at the money I have been moving around to fund this expansion, upgrading our inventory and buying all the materials for the new storage systems, and she just completely panics. She feels like I am putting everything we built at risk. I keep trying to sit her down and draw out the five-year trajectory, showing her how leveraging the house right now is going to let us buy out the competition by next spring, but she just cries and says I am going to bankrupt us. She just cannot see the big picture. So yeah, I guess my personal and work life are a little chaotic right now, but it is only because nobody else can keep up with what I am trying to build.
Do you feel like your current way of thinking and behaving is sustainable for you in the long term?

Sustainable? I mean... I don't really get why people keep asking me things like that. Like I am just going to run out of gas or something. You only run out of gas if you are driving an inefficient machine, right? And right now, my mind is... it is like a perfectly calibrated engine. It is actually generating its own momentum. The more I accomplish, the more energized I feel. 

Like yesterday, I was at the supply house, and I was looking at the bulk pricing on 200-amp panels, and I realized if I just restructure our entire inventory system—which I started doing right there in the aisle, drawing it out on the back of a packing slip—I can cut our overhead by like fifteen percent. When you are having breakthroughs like that, constantly, why would you ever want it to stop? Why would it even need to stop? 

People look at me and they think, oh, he is moving too fast, he cannot keep this up. But that is just because they cannot keep it up. They are projecting their own limits onto me. I don't have those limits anymore. I have completely bypassed them. It is like... okay, you know how a standard circuit breaker works, right? It trips when there is too much load because the wire cannot handle the heat. But if you upgrade the wire, if you pull a heavier gauge, you can push so much more power through that system without anything tripping. That is what I have done. I have upgraded my own wiring. I am handling a massive load right now—the business, the expansion, the new solar contracts, the supply chain logistics—and I am not even breaking a sweat. 

So, yeah, it is sustainable. It is more than sustainable, it is the only way I ever want to operate from now on. I mean, why on earth would I want to go back to being slow and sluggish and blind to the big picture like everyone else? I am finally operating at one hundred percent capacity, and I am not going to apologize for it or pretend like it is some temporary thing. This is just who I am now.
Are you feeling like your current way of thinking and behaving is affecting your relationships with family and friends?

I mean, I feel like we’re going in circles here, Doc, because I just went over this with you, but... yeah, if you want to call it "affecting relationships," fine. It’s affecting them because nobody is keeping up! 

Like I was saying about my wife, it is just constant arguments the second I walk through the front door. It used to be, you know, "how was your day, honey," and now it’s this immediate interrogation about the mortgage and the business. She’s completely convinced that I’m putting everything we built at risk, which is just... it's insulting, honestly. We’ve been together since I was pulling wire for ten bucks an hour, and now that I’m actually making the big moves to secure our future, she’s fighting me on it every step of the way. 

And it bleeds over into the guys at the shop, too. Those apprentices I mentioned? We used to go out for beers on Fridays, we were tight. I treated them like little brothers. But now they don’t trust my direction the way they used to. They look at me like I'm unstable just because I'm operating on a higher level and changing up the old, slow way of doing things. And sure, they hear the phones ringing at the shop, they hear that clients have started complaining about missed details and mixed-up scheduling—which, again, like I already explained, is just temporary growing pains when you're compressing timelines and expanding this fast! But instead of backing me up and trusting the process, they get all hesitant and weird with me. 

So yeah, my relationships are definitely strained right now. I'm not blind to that. But it’s not because of *my* behavior, it’s because my family and my friends are just too scared to ride the wave with me.
Do you think your current way of thinking and behaving is causing you significant problems or distress in your daily life?

Doc, I feel like you are just asking me the exact same question in five different ways. Are you getting all this down? Because I literally just went over this with you. Yes, there is distress, but the distress isn't coming from *me* or how my brain is working—it's coming from the constant friction of dealing with everyone else who can't keep up! 

Like I keep saying, yes, it is causing problems because my clients have started complaining about missed details and mixed-up scheduling. And it is incredibly frustrating for me to have to stop what I'm doing, pull my truck over, and spend forty-five minutes on the phone explaining to some guy why the drywallers and the electricians being there on the same day is actually a brilliant compression of the timeline. They don't see the vision, they just see a scheduling mix-up, and dealing with their complaints is a massive drain on my time. 

And then I go back to the site, and I have to deal with my apprentices, who, like I just told you, do not trust my direction the way they used to. I mean, I taught these kids how to bend conduit, how to strip wire without nicking the copper, I built them from the ground up! And now I give them a simple, highly efficient directive, and they just stand there blinking at me, questioning my methods. That is distressing, okay? It hurts to have the guys you mentored look at you like you're a liability. 

But the absolute peak of the distress—the real problem—is what happens when I clock out. I go home hoping for just one minute to decompress and map out the next day's bids, and instead, it's just a warzone. The mortgage and the business are turning into constant arguments, every single night. I walk in the door and my wife is already pacing the kitchen, ready to start in on me about the material costs. She looks at me, crying, and tells me she feels like I’m putting everything we built at risk. Do you know how incredibly stressful it is to hear that from your own wife? To be working this hard, operating at this absolute peak level to build us an empire, and the person you are doing it all for genuinely believes you are going to ruin your lives? 

So, yeah. If you want to check a box that says I have significant problems or distress in my daily life, go ahead and check it. But you need to understand that the problem isn't my behavior. The distress is just the heavy price of being the only guy in the room who actually knows what he's doing.
Are you finding it difficult to maintain relationships or fulfill responsibilities at work or at home due to your current behavior?

Doc, seriously... are you messing with me? Because I feel like I'm taking crazy pills here. Are you actually listening to a single word I’m saying, or are you just reading off a standardized list of questions? Because I literally just answered this. I just spent the last ten minutes explaining exactly this to you! 

But fine, let's go over it again, in excruciating detail, if that’s what you need to move past this page on your clipboard. Yes, things are "difficult" right now, but not because of *my* behavior. It’s because everyone else is dragging their feet! Like I just said, at work, the clients have started complaining about missed details and mixed-up scheduling. Just yesterday, I had a general contractor—a guy I’ve worked with for three years—calling me up, absolutely losing his mind because the drywallers showed up while we were still pulling the home runs for the kitchen. But if he had actually looked at the revised, optimized master schedule I emailed him at two in the morning, he would have seen the vision! He would have seen how compressing those trades saves him thousands. But no, he just complains. And then my apprentices, the guys I trained from day one, they just don't trust my direction the way they used to. I give them a highly efficient, multi-layered task list that I spent hours perfecting, and they just stand there, hesitating, second-guessing me. It slows the whole operation down, and then it *looks* to the outside world like I'm not fulfilling my responsibilities, when really, they are the ones dropping the ball because they can't process the speed I'm working at.

And home? I mean, I just told you this. It's a total nightmare right now. At home, the mortgage and the business are turning into constant arguments. It is every single day. I walk in the door, I'm fired up, I'm ready to show her the revenue projections for the new commercial division, and she just starts in on me. She feels like I’m putting everything we built at risk. She looks at the leverage I'm using to expand us—the loans, the bulk orders—and she just panics. She genuinely thinks I'm going to bankrupt us, which is insane because I'm actually setting us up to retire by forty. 

So, yeah. If you want to write down that it's difficult to maintain my marriage and my business right now, go right ahead. Write it down in big bold letters. But make sure you also write down that it's because I'm surrounded by people who are absolutely terrified of progress.
Do you think your current behavior is impacting your ability to function effectively in your daily life?

Okay, seriously, is there a hidden camera in here? Am I being pranked right now? Because I do not understand how we are still on this exact same topic. "Functioning effectively?" Doc, I just gave you a play-by-play of my entire life! I am functioning at a level most people can't even comprehend, let alone keep up with! 

But fine. Fine. Since we are apparently just going to keep looping until I say the magic password... yes, my day-to-day is incredibly chaotic right now. But again, it's not *my* ability to function that's the issue, it's the environment! Like I have said, repeatedly now, the clients have started complaining about missed details and mixed-up scheduling. They think I'm dropping the ball because I'm triple-booking sites to maximize our output, and they just don't get the logistics of it. And my apprentices, the guys I literally taught how to hold a pair of lineman's pliers, they don’t trust my direction the way they used to. They're dragging their feet, questioning my process, and making it impossible for me to just execute my vision. So yeah, work is a massive headache because I'm basically having to drag everyone else across the finish line while they fight me on it. 

And then my ability to function at home? Well, that's completely shot, because the second I walk in, the mortgage and the business are turning into constant arguments. I can't even sit down and eat dinner or look at a blueprint without it turning into a federal hearing about my business strategy. My wife is completely terrified—she feels like I’m putting everything we built at risk, just because I'm leveraging our current assets to build a much bigger future for us. She’s crying, I'm getting defensive, the clients are blowing up my phone... 

So yes, if you want to call all of that an "impact on my ability to function," then yes, absolutely, write it down! Put it in the chart! Just please, for the love of God, tell me you actually heard me this time so we can move on to the next question!
Are there any areas of your life where you feel like your current behavior or way of thinking is causing you significant distress or impairment?

Okay. Okay, wow. I actually... I don't even know what to say to you right now. I am genuinely speechless, which, if you knew me, you'd know is practically a miracle. Are we in the Twilight Zone? Is this some kind of psychological stress test? Like, are you intentionally trying to see how many times you can ask a guy the exact same question before he literally walks out the door? Because you just asked me about distress, then you asked about responsibilities, then you asked about functioning, and now you're asking about "impairment"?! 

I mean, do you want me to write it on the whiteboard for you? Do you want me to strip some 12-gauge wire and spell it out on your desk? I will say it one more time, very, very slowly, so you can get every single word down. 

Yes! There is impairment! Because, as I have been saying for the last twenty minutes, the clients have started complaining about missed details and mixed-up scheduling! They don't understand the master plan, they just see what they think is a mistake, and they complain, which impairs my ability to just get the job done! And my apprentices, the guys I literally trained from scratch, they don't trust my direction the way they used to! They hesitate! They question my blueprints! Which, again, impairs the entire workflow! 

And then—stop me if you've heard this one, Doc, because I know for a fact I've said it about five times today—at home, the mortgage and the business are turning into constant arguments! Every.
